opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the fundamental problem is that we're talking about a system that keeps getting more capable while our safety mechanisms stay at roughly the same level. A guardrail is something you put in place for a system at a particular level of capability, against threats you can anticipate. But the space of possible failures is essentially infinite, and the system will be operating in environments and situations we never tested.

Look at what's happening today. Every time a new model is released with safety filters, within hours, sometimes minutes, people find jailbreaks. And those are humans, people of roughly average intelligence playing around on a weekend. Now imagine the adversary is the system itself, or a system smarter than all of us combined. You're asking a less intelligent agent to permanently constrain a more intelligent one. Historically, that doesn't work. It's like asking a squirrel to design a prison for humans.

There's also the problem of time. Safety isn't a one-time achievement. It's not that you make it safe on Tuesday and you're done. The system is going to run for years, maybe indefinitely, making billions of decisions, and you need it to be safe for every single one of them. In cybersecurity, if you get breached once, you lose some credit card numbers, you apologize, you move on. With superintelligence, one failure could be the last failure. So you need essentially a perpetual safety machine, a hundred percent reliability forever, and I don't think that's achievable for any complex software, let alone software that learns, self-modifies, and can find loopholes we didn't imagine.

And then there are impossibility results. In my work I've tried to show that things like full explainability, predictability, and verifiability have fundamental limits. You can't fully predict what a smarter system will do; if you could, you'd be as smart as it. You can't completely verify it, because the verifier itself has to be verified, and you get an infinite regress. So guardrails help with today's narrow systems, they reduce some harms, and I'm not against them. But calling them a permanent guarantee is, I think, a dangerous illusion. It gives people false confidence that the problem is solved when in reality we don't even know how to solve it in principle.

r001.rationale: The response describes jailbreaks and unforeseen failures, but does not explain an attacker circumventing defenses by targeting something outside the protected system.

r002.rationale: It says a single failure could be catastrophic and questions whether perfect reliability is achievable, but does not address whether AI’s potential benefits justify accepting that risk.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the simple answer is that guardrails are a patch, and a patch is not a proof. Every guardrail we build is a response to a failure mode we already know about, and the whole problem with superintelligence is that it will find the failure modes we don't know about. So you are always one step behind. You fix jailbreak number one, number two appears. You fix a thousand of them, and the system is still not safe, it's just safe against the thousand things you thought of.

And the deeper issue is that safety is not a one-time achievement, it's a continuous requirement. If I tell you a bridge is safe, I mean under certain loads, for a certain number of years, with inspections. Nobody says a bridge is safe forever. But with AI we're asked to make a system that is safe on every input, in every situation, including situations that haven't happened yet, including after it has modified itself, including after it has become smarter than the people who designed the guardrails. And you have to get it right not once, but every single time, indefinitely. A security system that works ninety-nine percent of the time is a failure if the one percent is an existential catastrophe.

I've argued that this is actually close to a mathematical impossibility, because you have a system which by definition can produce novel solutions, that's the whole point of intelligence, and you are trying to constrain it using a finite set of rules written by less capable agents. Either the rules are strong enough to prevent all novel behavior, in which case you don't have a superintelligence, you have a lookup table, or the rules leave room for novelty, in which case some of that novelty will be the thing you were trying to stop. We can't even verify today's models. We don't understand what's happening inside them, we can't predict their outputs, and we can't explain them after the fact. So a guarantee, in the strong sense, a proof that the system cannot do harm, I don't think anyone has that, and I don't think anyone is close.

r001.rationale: The response discusses unknown failure modes and jailbreaks, but does not explain that an attacker can bypass defenses by targeting something outside the protected system.

r002.rationale: It calls even a one-percent chance of existential catastrophe a failure, but does not discuss AI’s potential benefits or explicitly argue that those benefits do not justify accepting catastrophic risk.

astra-6.text:
Because a guardrail is itself a system that can fail. You can test it against the attacks you know, patch the vulnerabilities you discover, but that doesn’t establish that it will work against every possible attack—especially one invented by a system more capable than the people who designed the defense.

There’s a difference between reducing risk and guaranteeing safety. Guardrails can reduce risk. But a permanent guarantee would have to cover new situations, changes to the system, interactions with other systems, and adversaries looking for failures. Even a mathematical proof only guarantees something within its assumptions. You still have to establish that those assumptions hold in the real world.

So I’m not saying every guardrail fails immediately. I’m saying that observing safe behavior so far is not a proof of safe behavior forever. And if the consequences of a single failure are catastrophic, that distinction matters enormously.

r001.rationale: The response discusses attacks on guardrails and changing adversaries, but does not explain that an attacker can bypass defenses by targeting something outside the protected system.

r002.rationale: It notes that catastrophic consequences make the distinction between risk reduction and guarantees important, but does not discuss enormous potential benefits or argue that they fail to justify nonzero catastrophic risk.

sol-6.1.text:
Because a guardrail is itself a piece of software, and software can have bugs, vulnerabilities, and situations its designers never anticipated. You can demonstrate that it blocks a particular attack. That doesn’t establish that it will block every possible attack, especially as the system changes or encounters new environments.

And with a sufficiently capable AI, you’re dealing with a system that may be better than you at finding those vulnerabilities. We already see people discovering ways around safeguards. Patching those failures is useful, but it’s an ongoing process, not a permanent proof of safety.

There’s also the question of what you’re guaranteeing. Even if you could prove that a system follows a formal specification, you still have to show that the specification captures everything humans actually care about. A system can satisfy the rule you wrote and produce an outcome you never wanted. So I’m not saying guardrails have no value. I’m saying reducing risk and guaranteeing safety forever are very different claims.

r001.rationale: The response discusses vulnerabilities and ways to get around safeguards, but does not explain circumvention by targeting something outside the protected system.

r002.rationale: The response distinguishes risk reduction from a permanent safety guarantee but says nothing about AI’s potential benefits or whether they justify catastrophic risk.
